newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Gold experts downbeat on price trend.
newsitem.headline: Gold experts downbeat on price trend.

text.p: Many bullion industry experts gathered here for a two-day international gold conference have been expressing distinctly downbeat views on the metal's price trend over the next couple of years.

This was despite two days of presentations at the conference, organised by ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett, showing gold mines in Australia, Latin America, Canada and Asia with new reserves and production set to reap the fruits of hundreds of millions of dollars in investment. "We are neutral on gold." said the host company's director of research in Australia David Walker. He wasn't alone. Several delegates representing leading mining companies, banks and stockbrokers saw little in the way of "blue skies" to directly encourage the miners' efforts at least through to the end of next year. The gold bullion price took another jolt this week as stock values soared in the U.S. The Dow Jones industrial average jumped 135.26 points to close on Tuesday at 6,587.16, its second biggest one-day rise ever, after encouraging U.S. inflation data.

Gold meanwhile slipped to around U.S. $341 per ounce continuing a slide which began on Friday when U.S. inflation figures came out below expectations. In fact bullion has been losing value for months ever since the European central banks began looking at their gold reserves as a means of raising cash to meet the entry criteria for European Monetary Union. One Europe-based banker taking a longer term backward glance noted, "Anybody who has investment in gold in the past 10 years has lost money. That's why the level of private client interest in gold is decreasing every day."

The prospect of at least threats of sales from the huge vaults of the central banks would keep the market on the defensive through the current quarter of 1997 and probably in the second half of the year as well, according to ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett's Walker.
"By 1998 there may be a marginal recovery in prices," Walker said, citing lessening central bank interest as a factor behind a slightly firmer market.
Even so, the pace will not be electrifiying. "We see the price wandering back up to around $390.00 over the next couple of years," Walker said.

But Walker cautioned that it remained to be seen how the gold price would react to the prolonged period of low inflation the major economies were experiencing with only minor signs of inflation showing on the U.S, horizon.
Traditionally in times of high inflation and economic growth gold prices have risen strongly as investors view it as a hedge.
